title: Retrospective: Data Mining Static Code Attributes to Learn Defect Predictors

edges.target: PROMISE repository (NASA defect data: CM1, JM1, KC1, PC1, ...)
edges.ref: http://tiny.cc/promise25 ; Seacraft at https://zenodo.org/communities/seacraft
edges.evidence: we built mutators that injected an increasing amount of their quality issues into PROMISE defect data sets. Strangely, the performance curve remained flat
edges.section: 5.2 Stranger Things (Menzies's 6th Law); footnote 8 lists CM1, JM1, KC1...PC5

edges.target: Shepperd et al. NASA data quality issues (repeated rows, illegal attributes)
edges.ref: [89] M. Shepperd, Q. Song, Z. Sun, C. Mair, Data quality: Some comments on the nasa software defect datasets, TSE 39(9), 2013
edges.evidence: But they never tested if increasing their kinds of quality issues decreased the predictive power of learned models. To address that, we built mutators that injected an increasing amount of their quality issues

edges.target: Cohen 'straw man' benchmarking guidance (Empirical Methods for AI)
edges.ref: [94] P. R. Cohen, Empirical methods for artificial intelligence. MIT press, 1995
edges.evidence: Cohen argues that supposedly sophisticated methods should be benchmarked against seemingly stupider ones (the so-called "straw man" approach to scientific verification)

edges.target: Hou et al. SLR of LLMs for SE (229 papers)
edges.ref: [81] X. Hou et al., Large language models for software engineering: A systematic literature review, TOSEM 33(8), 2024
edges.evidence: in a recent systematic review [81] of 229 SE papers using large language models (LLMs), only 13/229 = 5% of those papers compared LLMs to other approaches

edges.target: Grinsztajn et al. tree models beat deep learning on tabular data
edges.ref: [82] L. Grinsztajn, E. Oyallon, G. Varoquaux, Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data? NeurIPS'22
edges.evidence: other methods (developed and certified using PROMISE-style research) can produce results that are better and/or faster [82]-[88]

edges.target: Herbold et al. problems with SZZ / defect data collection
edges.ref: [53] S. Herbold, A. Trautsch, F. Trautsch, B. Ledel, Problems with szz and features..., EMSE 27(2), 2022
edges.evidence: little curation, little validation, often purely heuristic data collection without quality checks... all this newer data might not necessarily be better [52], [53]

edges.target: Menzies, Greenwald & Frank 2007 defect-prediction results (feature pruning, static attributes beat baselines)
edges.ref: [1] T. Menzies, J. Greenwald, A. Frank, Data mining static code attributes to learn defect predictors, TSE 33(1), pp. 2-13, 2007
edges.evidence: For a set of three dozen metrics, and seven data sets, pruning selected just two or three attributes

edges.target: Wan et al. survey of 395 practitioners on defect prediction
edges.ref: [19] Z. Wan, X. Xia, A. E. Hassan, D. Lo, J. Yin, X. Yang, Perceptions, expectations, & challenges in defect prediction, TSE, 2018
edges.evidence: In their 2018 survey of 395 commercial practitioners from 33 countries and five continents, Wan et al. [19] found that over 90% of the respondents were willing to adopt defect prediction techniques

edges.target: Misirli et al. telecom defect predictor case study
edges.ref: [11] A. T. Misirli, A. Bener, R. Kale, Ai-based software defect predictors: Applications and benefits in a case study, AI Magazine, 2011
edges.evidence: Their models predicted 87% of code defects and decreased inspection efforts by 72% (while reducing post-release defects by 44%)

edges.target: Kim et al. REMI defect prediction at Samsung
edges.ref: [20] M. Kim, J. Nam, J. Yeon, S. Choi, S. Kim, Remi: defect prediction for efficient api testing, FSE, 2015
edges.evidence: Their models could predict the bug-prone APIs with reasonable accuracy (0.68 F1 scores) and reduce the resources required for executing test cases

edges.target: Rahman et al. static bug finders vs statistical defect prediction
edges.ref: [18] F. Rahman, S. Khatri, E. T. Barr, P. Devanbu, Comparing static bug finders and statistical prediction, ICSE, 2014
edges.evidence: compared (a) static code analysis tools FindBugs, Jlint, and PMD with (b) defect predictors... built using logistic regression. No significant differences in cost-effectiveness were observed

edges.target: Ostrand, Weyuker & Bell 'Where the bugs are' (defects unevenly distributed)
edges.ref: [10] T. J. Ostrand, E. J. Weyuker, R. M. Bell, Where the bugs are, ACM SIGSOFT SEN, 2004
edges.evidence: Software bugs are not evenly distributed across a project [8]-[11]. Hence, a useful way to test software is to allocate most assessment budgets to the more defect-prone parts

edges.target: Hamill & Goseva-Popstojanova common trends in fault data
edges.ref: [8] M. Hamill, K. Goseva-Popstojanova, Common trends in software fault and failure data, TSE, 2009
edges.evidence: Software bugs are not evenly distributed across a project [8]-[11]

edges.target: Koru et al. functional form of size-defect relationship
edges.ref: [9] A. G. Koru, D. Zhang, K. El Emam, H. Liu, An investigation into the functional form of the size-defect relationship for software modules, TSE, 2009
edges.evidence: Software bugs are not evenly distributed across a project [8]-[11]

edges.target: Fu, Menzies & Shen: assessment effectiveness grows exponentially with effort
edges.ref: [7] W. Fu, T. Menzies, X. Shen, Tuning for software analytics: Is it really necessary? IST, 2016
edges.evidence: This is useful since software quality assurance budgets are finite while assessment effectiveness increases exponentially with effort [7]

edges.target: Shepperd & Ince: static code measures are just a proxy for lines of code
edges.ref: [16] M. Shepperd, D. Ince, A critique of three metrics, JSS 26(3), pp. 197-210, 1994
edges.evidence: Sheppard and Ince [16] had correlation results showing that "for a large class of software (static code measures) are no more than a proxy for, and in many cases outperformed by, lines of code."

edges.target: Fenton & Pfleeger: uselessness of static code attributes
edges.ref: [15] N. E. Fenton, S. Pfleeger, Software Metrics: A Rigorous and Practical Approach, International Thompson Press, 1997
edges.evidence: Fenton and Pfleeger had examples of the same functionality achieved via different language constructs resulting in different static measurements [15]. They used these examples to argue the uselessness of static code attributes

edges.target: Turhan et al. cross-company defect prediction (Turkish white goods -> NASA)
edges.ref: [67] B. Turhan, T. Menzies, A. B. Bener, J. Di Stefano, On the relative value of cross-company and within-company data for defect prediction, EMSE 14, pp. 540-578, 2009
edges.evidence: consider transfer learning research [67] where models from Turkish white goods were successful at predicting errors in NASA systems

edges.target: Pan & Yang survey on transfer learning (complex multi-dimensional transform)
edges.ref: [68] S. J. Pan, Q. Yang, A survey on transfer learning, IEEE TKDE 22(10), pp. 1345-1359, 2009
edges.evidence: Transfer learning is often seen as complex multi-dimensional transform that maps attributes in one domain to another [68]. But for defect prediction, all that was needed was some simple nearest neighboring

edges.target: Manifold assumption (Zhu semi-supervised learning survey)
edges.ref: [74] X. Zhu, Semi-supervised learning literature survey, Computer Sciences TR 1530, 2005
edges.evidence: Readers familiar with the manifold assumption [74] and the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma [75] will be nodding sagely at this point - but the reductions seen in SE data are startling

edges.target: Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma
edges.ref: [75] W. B. Johnson, J. Lindenstrauss, Extensions of lipschitz mappings into a hilbert space, Contemporary Mathematics 26, pp. 189-206, 1984
edges.evidence: Readers familiar with the manifold assumption [74] and the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma [75] will be nodding sagely at this point - but the reductions seen in SE data are startling

edges.target: Tu & Menzies FRUGAL semi-supervised learning (labels ignored for most data)
edges.ref: [66] H. Tu, T. Menzies, Frugal: unlocking semi-supervised learning for software analytics, ASE'22, pp. 394-406, 2022
edges.evidence: found they could predict for Github issue close time, effort estimation, and defect prediction, even after ignoring labels for 80%, 91%, 97%, 98%, 100% (respectively) of their project data labels [66], [71]-[73], [76]

edges.target: Kocaguneli et al. active learning and effort estimation (essential content)
edges.ref: [71] E. Kocaguneli, T. Menzies, J. Keung, D. Cok, R. Madachy, Active learning and effort estimation: Finding the essential content of software effort estimation data, TSE 39(8), pp. 1040-1053, 2013
edges.evidence: even after ignoring labels for 80%, 91%, 97%, 98%, 100% (respectively) of their project data labels [66], [71]-[73], [76]

edges.target: Peters, Menzies & Layman LACE2 privacy-preserving data sharing
edges.ref: [72] F. Peters, T. Menzies, L. Layman, Lace2: Better privacy-preserving data sharing for cross project defect prediction, ICSE 2015, pp. 801-811
edges.evidence: even after ignoring labels for 80%, 91%, 97%, 98%, 100% (respectively) of their project data labels [66], [71]-[73], [76]

edges.target: Chen et al. finding the right data for software cost modeling
edges.ref: [73] Z. Chen, T. Menzies, D. Port, D. Boehm, Finding the right data for software cost modeling, IEEE Software 22(6), pp. 38-46, 2005
edges.evidence: even after ignoring labels for 80%, 91%, 97%, 98%, 100% (respectively) of their project data labels [66], [71]-[73], [76]

edges.target: Xu et al. clustering-based unsupervised defect prediction (100% labels ignored)
edges.ref: [76] Z. Xu, L. Li, M. Yan, J. Liu, X. Luo, J. Grundy, Y. Zhang, X. Zhang, A comprehensive comparative study of clustering-based unsupervised defect prediction models, JSS 172, 110862, 2021
edges.evidence: even after ignoring labels for 80%, 91%, 97%, 98%, 100% (respectively) of their project data labels [66], [71]-[73], [76]

edges.target: Menzies et al. ceiling effects in defect predictors (few dozen samples suffice)
edges.ref: [77] T. Menzies, B. Turhan, A. Bener, G. Gay, B. Cukic, Y. Jiang, Implications of ceiling effects in defect predictors, PROMISE'08, pp. 47-54
edges.evidence: Data sets with thousands of rows can be modeled with just a few dozen samples [77]

edges.target: Lin & Whitehead power laws in fine-grained code changes
edges.ref: [78] Z. Lin, J. Whitehead, Why power laws? an explanation from fine-grained code changes, MSR 2015, pp. 68-75
edges.evidence: perhaps because of power laws [78] or large amounts of repeated structures [79] in the data from SE projects

edges.target: Hindle et al. naturalness of software (repeated structures)
edges.ref: [79] A. Hindle, E. T. Barr, Z. Su, M. Gabel, P. Devanbu, On the naturalness of software, ICSE'12, pp. 837-847
edges.evidence: perhaps because of power laws [78] or large amounts of repeated structures [79] in the data from SE projects

edges.target: Majumder et al. 500+ times faster than deep learning
edges.ref: [85] S. Majumder, N. Balaji, K. Brey, W. Fu, T. Menzies, 500+ times faster than deep learning, MSR 2018
edges.evidence: other methods (developed and certified using PROMISE-style research) can produce results that are better and/or faster [82]-[88]

edges.target: Fu & Menzies Easy over hard (simple SVM+DE vs deep learning)
edges.ref: [87] W. Fu, T. Menzies, Easy over hard: a case study on deep learning, ESEC/FSE 2017, pp. 49-60
edges.evidence: other methods (developed and certified using PROMISE-style research) can produce results that are better and/or faster [82]-[88]

edges.target: Nair et al. bad learners find good configurations (poor predictors still rank well)
edges.ref: [90] V. Nair, T. Menzies, N. Siegmund, S. Apel, Using bad learners to find good configurations, FSE 2017
edges.evidence: Nair et al. [90] found that models that predicted poorly could still rank one solution over another. Hence, they can be used to (e.g.) prune away poor configurations

edges.target: Agrawal & Menzies tuning SMOTE (better data vs better data miners)
edges.ref: [34] A. Agrawal, T. Menzies, Is better data better than better data miners?: on the benefits of tuning smote for defect prediction, ICSE 2018
edges.evidence: One of the lessons of hyperparameter optimization [34], [91]-[93] on PROMISE data is that conclusions reached via data mining can be changed and made more accurate, in an afternoon

edges.target: Agrawal et al. DODGE (how to 'dodge' complex software analytics)
edges.ref: [91] A. Agrawal, W. Fu, D. Chen, X. Shen, T. Menzies, How to "dodge" complex software analytics? TSE, 2019
edges.evidence: conclusions reached via data mining can be changed and made more accurate, in an afternoon, by a grad student with enough CPU

edges.target: Tantithamthavorn et al. automated parameter optimization for defect prediction
edges.ref: [92] C. Tantithamthavorn, S. McIntosh, A. E. Hassan, K. Matsumoto, Automated parameter optimization of classification techniques for defect prediction models, ICSE 2016
edges.evidence: conclusions reached via data mining can be changed and made more accurate, in an afternoon, by a grad student with enough CPU

edges.target: Fu, Menzies & Shen tuning for software analytics
edges.ref: [93] W. Fu, T. Menzies, X. Shen, Tuning for software analytics, IST 76, pp. 135-146, 2016
edges.evidence: And more often than not, a year later, I have switched to the simpler approach [34], [91]-[93]

edges.target: Robles: replicability of MSR papers
edges.ref: [5] G. Robles, Replicating MSR: A study of the potential replicability of papers published in the mining software repositories proceedings, MSR 2010, pp. 171-180
edges.evidence: Typically, MSR publications did not prioritize revisiting datasets already analyzed in previous work [5] (a trend that has improved, only somewhat [6])

edges.target: Gonzalez-Barahona & Robles: revisiting reproducibility of repository-based empirical SE
edges.ref: [6] J. M. Gonzalez-Barahona, G. Robles, Revisiting the reproducibility of empirical software engineering studies based on data retrieved from development repositories, IST 164, 107318, 2023
edges.evidence: Typically, MSR publications did not prioritize revisiting datasets already analyzed in previous work [5] (a trend that has improved, only somewhat [6])

notes: Retrospective on the 2007 TSE paper and PROMISE; only executed reuse is the Shepperd-issues mutator study on PROMISE data (re-typed replication, polarity refutes); most new edges are prior measurements quoted as premises for 'Menzies's Laws', plus manifold/J-L theory and three refutation-polarity edges (Shepperd & Ince, Fenton & Pfleeger, Pan & Yang).
